summary: Documents a simple experiment of a TCP sender using a four-packet start toward a receiver behind a 9600 bps modem link with only three buffers. The finding was that no significant degradation was seen compared with a smaller start. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP normally starts a new connection by sending one packet and waiting for it to be acknowledged. Sending four packets at once would reach full speed sooner, but on a slow modem link with only three buffers the fourth packet would be thrown away. This memo reports a simulation that compared the two ways of starting, and found that the four-packet start was not worse.

questions: what happens when tcp sends four packets into three buffers
does a larger tcp initial window hurt slow links
does a four packet tcp start hurt slow modem links
what is the tcp four packet start

how did the four packet start perform in the simulation
subtitle: A simulation showing that a TCP connection starting with four packets is not worse on a slow modem link than starting with one.

tldr.problem: A proposal to let TCP begin a connection by sending four packets instead of one worried operators of slow modem links, where a router holding only three buffers would certainly drop the fourth packet.
tldr.mechanism: The authors simulated a path of a 100 Mbps link, a 1.5 Mbps link with 25 ms of delay and a 9600 bps modem link with 150 ms of delay, with three buffers before the modem, and compared a one-packet start with a four-packet start using four TCP variants.
tldr.outcome: No significant degradation was measured. The four-packet start ended up about 0.229 seconds ahead of the one-packet start, and the memo reports the result as a simulation while leaving open whether the change is safe for the network as a whole.

facts.label: Time to send three segments at 9600 bps

today: RFC 2416 is an Informational memo from September 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It reports one simulation of one scenario, and its own authors say the result would need to be repeated with real TCP implementations and real modems before it could settle the question.

sections.title: The Proposal and the Worry
sections.content:
Sally Floyd proposed that TCP begin its initial slow start by sending as many as four packets, instead of the usual one. The aim is to get TCP up to speed faster. A slow start that follows a timeout would still begin with a single packet. Starting with more than one packet might reduce the start-up latency over long, fat pipes by two round-trip times. The proposal is documented separately, and the memo assumes the reader is familiar with it.

On the end2end-interest mailing list, concern was raised about a case said to be common: a slow modem served by a router which allocates only three buffers per modem, one buffer being transmitted while two packets wait. In that arrangement, starting with four packets would not be good, because the fourth packet is sure to be dropped.

Vern Paxson replied that the four-packet start is no worse than what happens after two round-trip times in normal slow start, so no new problem is introduced by starting with as many as four packets. If there is a problem with a four-packet start, then the problem already exists in a normal slow-start start-up after two round-trip times, when the slow-start algorithm releases four closely spaced packets into the network. The experiment reported in the memo confirmed Paxson's reasoning.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting a connection with four packets instead of one would save time on long links. The worry was that a slow modem with room for only three packets would simply throw the fourth one away, so the change would make things worse rather than better. The answer was that ordinary slow start already sends four packets close together once it is under way, so the four-packet start only moves that moment earlier.

sections.title: The Experimental Setup
sections.content:
The scenario consists of three links between the source and the sink. The first link is a 100 Mbps link with no delay, connecting the sender to a router. It was included to have a means of logging the returning acknowledgements at the time they would be seen by the sender. The second link is a 1.5 Mbps link with a 25 ms one-way delay, included to roughly model traversing an uncongested, intra-continental piece of the terrestrial Internet. The third link is a 9600 bps link with a 150 ms one-way delay, connecting the edge of the net to a receiver that is behind the modem.

The queue limits for the queues at each end of the first two links were set to 100, a value sufficiently large that this limit was never a factor. The queue limits at each end of the 9600 bps link were set to 3 packets, which can hold at most two packets while one is being sent.

Version 1.2a2 of the NS simulator was used to simulate both one-packet and four-packet starts for each of the available TCP algorithms: tahoe, reno, sack and fack. The conclusion reported is independent of which TCP algorithm is used, in general. In the four-packet start cases the window-init variable was set to 4, and the TCP implementations were modified to use the value of the window-init variable only on connection start, but to set cwnd to 1 on other instances of a slow start. The packets in simulation are 1024 bytes long, for purposes of determining the time it takes to transmit them through the links. The TCP modules included with the simulator do not simulate the TCP sequence number mechanisms; they use just packet numbers. Observations are made of all packets and acknowledgements crossing the 100 Mbps no-delay link, near the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: The test used a fast link, then a moderately fast link with a quarter of a second of delay, and finally a 9600 bit per second modem link with a third of a second of delay. The router feeding the modem had room for only three packets. The researchers ran both kinds of start with four different TCP versions in a network simulator, and watched the traffic near the sender.

sections.title: The Two Traces
sections.content:
With normal slow start, packet number 1 is sent at time 0.0. An acknowledgement covering packet number 1 arrives at time 1.222, and packets 2 and 3 are sent. An acknowledgement covering packet number 2 arrives at time 2.444, and packets 4 and 5 are sent. An acknowledgement covering packet number 3 arrives at time 3.278, and packets 6 and 7 are sent. The pattern continues: acknowledgements covering packet 4 at time 4.111, packet 5 at time 4.944 and packet 6 at time 5.778, each releasing two more packets.

At time 6.111 a duplicate acknowledgement is received, again covering packet number 6. Another arrives at time 7.444. At time 8.278 a third duplicate acknowledgement is received, covering packet number 6, and packet number 7 is retransmitted.

With a four-packet start, packets 1, 2, 3 and 4 are all sent at time 0.0. An acknowledgement covering packet number 1 arrives at time 1.222 and packets 5 and 6 are sent. Acknowledgements covering packet number 2 and packet number 3 arrive at times 2.055 and 2.889, and packets 7 and 8, then 9 and 10, are sent. At time 3.722 a duplicate acknowledgement is received covering packet number 3, another at time 4.555, and at time 5.389 a third duplicate acknowledgement covering packet number 3 is received and packet number 4 is retransmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: In the ordinary case the sender sends one packet, waits, then sends two more each time an acknowledgement comes back. In the four-packet case it sends four at once and then carries on in the same way. Both runs lose a packet to the three-buffer queue in front of the modem, and both recover by retransmitting it after three duplicate acknowledgements.

sections.title: What the Traces Show
sections.content:
At the point where the two traces stop being written out, the two systems are in almost identical states. The traces from that point on are almost the same, modulo a shift in time of 8.278 minus 5.389, which is 2.889 seconds, and a shift of three packets. If the normal TCP with the one-packet start delivers packet N at time T, then the TCP with the four-packet start delivers packet N minus 3 at time T minus 2.889 seconds.

The time to send three 1024-byte TCP segments through a 9600 bps modem is 2.66 seconds. So the four-packet-start TCP delivers packet N at time T minus 2.889 plus 2.66, which is T minus 0.229, in most cases, and in some cases earlier and in some cases later, because different packets, by number, experience loss in the two traces. The four-packet-start TCP is therefore about 0.229 seconds, roughly one fifth of a packet, ahead of where the one-packet-start TCP would be. The memo attributes this to the extra time the modem sits idle while waiting for the dally timer to go off in the receiver in the one-packet-start case.

The states of the two systems are not exactly identical. They differ slightly in the round-trip-time estimators, because the behaviour at the start is not identical. The observed round trip times may differ by a small amount due to dally timers, and due to the one-packet start experiencing more round trip times before the first loss. In the cases where a retransmit timer did later go off, the additional difference in timing was much smaller than the 0.229 second difference described above.
sections.plainLanguage: After the first loss the two runs look the same, only shifted: the four-packet run is 2.889 seconds ahead in time and three packets ahead in sequence. Sending those three extra packets over the modem takes 2.66 seconds, so the four-packet run finishes about 0.229 seconds ahead. The difference comes from the modem sitting idle waiting for the receiver's acknowledgement delay, which the four-packet run does not have to wait for.

sections.title: Conclusion and Open Questions
sections.content:
In this particular case, the four-packet start is not harmful.

The authors add that a four-packet start would be very helpful in situations where a long-delay link is involved, because it would reduce transfer times for moderately-sized transfers by as much as two round-trip times. But it remains, in their opinion at the time, an open question whether the four-packet start would be safe for the network.

They also note that it would be good to see whether this result could be duplicated with real TCP implementations, real modems and real three-buffer limits, rather than a simulation.
sections.plainLanguage: In the situation tested, starting with four packets did no harm. The authors think it would help a lot on links with long delays, but they say it was still an open question whether it would be safe for the Internet as a whole, and that the result should be repeated with real software and real modems.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section explains that it discusses a simulation study of the effects of a proposed change to TCP, so there are no security considerations directly related to the document. It adds that there are also no known security considerations associated with the proposed change.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing to report here. The memo is a simulation study of a proposed change to TCP, and the change itself has no known security implications.
